title: Kabir's saloks
hookLine: near the Granth's end come over two hundred short couplets of Kabir, sharp and funny (ang 1364–1377)
last: KABIR — WHAT THEY FEAR, I WELCOME.

cards: A proverb a grandmother said once that nobody in the family forgot. A line on a sticky note on the fridge. Two sentences someone posts that get screenshotted and passed around.
Short things stick, because they can be carried.
Near the end of the Guru Granth Sahib there's a whole run of Kabir's short sayings, two lines each, a couple of hundred of them, some tender, some sharp enough to sting, some genuinely funny.
Today's word is what they're called: salok.

teach.b: A salok is a short verse, usually a couplet; the word comes from the Sanskrit shloka.
Kabir's saloks fill the pages from Ang 1364 to 1377, more than two hundred of them. A few, marked with the Gurus' names, are replies or comments by Guru Amar Das and Guru Arjan, tucked in among his.
Each usually opens with his own name, Kabir, like a signature on a postcard. Here are three, in paraphrase. The very first: Kabir, my rosary is my tongue, and on it is God's Name.
No beads needed; the prayer is in how you speak. Another: Kabir, I'm the worst of all; everyone else is good. Whoever understands it this way is my friend.
A joke with a point: the quickest way to stop judging people is to start with yourself.
And another: a true saint doesn't give up goodness even among a crowd of bad people, just as the sandalwood tree, wrapped in snakes, never stops being cool and fragrant. Notice the pattern.
Each takes one ordinary picture, a rosary, a judge, a tree, and flips it.
They're built to be memorized, quoted at the right moment, to sting a little and then stay with you.
Some people keep a handful by heart, the way others keep proverbs. You don't have to read all two hundred. Three, carried well, will do.

how: Kabir's saloks are read near the end of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and some are quoted like proverbs.

games.q: you're about to judge someone harshly. which of Kabir's saloks fits the moment?
o: I'm the worst of all; everyone else is good.
games.why: Kabir's joke with a point: start with yourself, and judging others gets much harder.

practice: Take the three into the quiet, one at a time: my rosary is my tongue, and notice how you've spoken today; I'm the worst of all, and let one judgment you're carrying soften; the sandalwood stays cool among snakes, and picture yourself staying kind in one hard place.
